## Case 1: "Just send a quick summary" {.smaller .scrollable}

A cardiology department at a regional hospital has been collaborating with a
pharmaceutical company developing a new diagnostic support tool for chest pain
patients. Before deciding whether to include your hospital in a larger clinical
trial, the company asks for a quick baseline summary of your recent patients:

> "Nothing complicated --- just basic descriptive numbers so our statisticians
> can take a look."

You are given a dataset of 303 patients admitted with chest pain (age,
cholesterol, blood pressure, heart rate, etc.), along with whether they were
later confirmed to have coronary artery disease. Your supervisor tells you:

> "This is not a statistics task --- we just need simple summaries like average
> values and variability for key variables. The statisticians will handle the
> rest."

Later that day, you receive a follow-up email:

> "Please report mean and standard deviation for age, cholesterol, resting blood
> pressure, and max heart rate, stratified by heart disease status. We need it
> today to decide whether your site qualifies."

The data is stored in `.csv` format and the company has provided you access to a
GDPR-friendly and secure server where all the company data are stored. The only
software installed on the server is `R` and `RStudio`.

## Case 1: "Just send a quick summary" {.center}

- Any questions about words?
- Is the task clear?
- What skills will you need to master in order to do it?

## Let's practice reading some figures {.center style="text-align: center;"}

## What do you make of this plot?

```{r}
#| label: first-plot
#| echo: false

# output-location: slide

data(hd_data, package = "medisr")

hd_data |>
  ggauto::ggauto(
    HD,
    MaxHR,
    title = "Coronary Heart Disease",
    subtitle = "303 individuals (139 Yes, 164 No) measured.",
    caption = "**Source**: Cleveland Medical Center",
    xlab = "Max Hear Rate",
    ylab = "Coronary Heart Disease"
  )
```

## What about this one?

```{r}
#| label: second-plot
#| echo: false

# output-location: slide

hd_data |>
  ggauto::ggauto(
    Age,
    MaxHR,
    title = "Coronary Heart Disease",
    subtitle = "303 individuals (139 Yes, 164 No) measured.",
    caption = "**Source**: Cleveland Medical Center",
    xlab = "Age",
    ylab = "Max Hear Rate"
  )
```

## What can we learn from data? {.r-stretch .r-fit-text}

::: {.fragment}
- We saw how max heart rate vary between patients having coronary heart
  disease...
:::

::: {.fragment}
- We saw how max heart rate change across peoples age...
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Now, could it just be that the patients with coronary heart disease are older?
- **Let's make a plot and check together!**
:::

## Exploring the Heart Disease dataset

1) Go to
   [**https://danmazjen.github.io/medicinsk-statistik**](https://danmazjen.github.io/medicinsk-statistik),
   exercises, and find the Cleveland Heart Disease dataset

2) Copy the following code:

```r
data(hd_data, package = "medisr")
```

3) Past it into your R console and check if you see the data in your `variable`
   pane.

## Code-along {auto-animate="true"}

```r
library(ggplot2)                                # <1>

hd_data                                       # <2>
```

1. Tell R you will be using the `ggplot2` package
2. Take `hd_data`, and then,

## Code-along {auto-animate="true"}

```r
library(ggplot2)                                # <1>

hd_data |>                                      # <2>
  ggplot(                                        # <3>
    aes(x = HD, y = Age)                    # <4>
    ) +                                          # <5>
  geom_boxplot()                                 # <6>
```

1. Tell R you will be using the `ggplot2` package
2. Take `hd_data`, and then,
3. Make a `ggplot` skeleton
4. Select the x and y variables using `aes` (aestetics)
5. End the ggplot function that has a parenthesis open. Add `+` more...
6. Specify the type of plot you want `ggplot` to do with the skeleton

## You made your first plot with R code! 🎉🥳

```{r}
#| label: first-plot-celebrate
#| echo: false

library(ggplot2)                                # <1>

hd_data |>                                      # <2>
  ggplot(                                        # <3>
    aes(x = HD, y = Age)                    # <4>
    ) +                                          # <5>
  geom_boxplot()                                 # <6>
```

# Medical Statistics

In this course, we will

- develop statistical literacy skills
- Learn to make medical inference from statistics
- Perform statistics with the help of **R**

## Develop statistical literacy skills

::: {.fragment}
- Interpret results from medical studies (e.g. *p*-values, confidence intervals,
  effect sizes)
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Critically evaluate claims in clinical research and media
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Identify common statistical pitfalls and misleading conclusions
:::

## Learn to make medical inference from statistics

::: {.fragment}
- Translate statistical results into clinically meaningful conclusions
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Understand uncertainty and variability in patient outcomes
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Statistical significance does not equal clinical importance --- ask whether
  the result would actually change patient care
:::

## Perform statistics using R

::: {.fragment}
- Plotting data using `ggplot2` as you've already experienced
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Run statistical tests such as t-test, regression, etc.
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Read and understand the `R` output
:::
